title: Succession Looks Different When the Business Belongs to a Community, Not One Founder
linkedin:
Succession planning advice almost always assumes one founder, one business, and eventually a trade sale.

For Indigenous-owned enterprises and social enterprises, that assumption doesn't hold, and treating succession as one single decision is usually where the planning stalls.

Ownership in these organisations often sits with a community, a trust or a board representing several family groups. That means succession usually needs to split into two separate tracks. Operational succession, who runs the business day to day, can move on a fairly normal timeline. Governance succession, who holds signing authority and who the organisation's funders and corporate partners actually deal with, runs on a completely different clock, set by community process rather than one person's retirement date.

The relationship risk sits in a place most boards don't expect. Funders and corporate partners holding Indigenous procurement targets have often built their trust with the founding leader personally, over many years. None of that transfers just because a new name appears on a letterhead.

Even though most of these organisations aren't heading toward a trade sale, valuation still matters. A board still needs a defensible number to make sound calls on reinvestment, debt capacity and any buyout owed to a leader stepping back, rather than a guess carried in one person's head.

The organisations that handle this well start the conversation years before the founder actually intends to step back, while that person can still make the introductions personally.

Full piece on the ProfitPulse blog.

Quick thought for anyone on the board of a community-owned or mission-driven organisation.

Most succession advice assumes one founder and one eventual buyer. That doesn't really apply here, ownership usually sits with a community or a trust, not one person.

But the risk is still real. Funders and corporate partners often trust the founding leader personally, built up over years, and that trust doesn't automatically transfer just because a new name appears on a letterhead.

For board members and leaders of Indigenous-owned enterprises and social enterprises across Queensland, New South Wales and Victoria, a quick note on a planning gap we see come up often.

Most succession advice is written for a business with one owner heading toward a trade sale. That doesn't map well onto an organisation where ownership sits with a community, a trust or a board representing several family groups. Succession here usually needs to be split into two separate decisions, who runs the organisation day to day, and who holds governance and signing authority, since those two often move on very different timelines.

The part boards miss most often is relationships. Funders and corporate partners frequently trust the founding leader personally, built up over years of direct contact, and that trust has to be actively handed over through introductions, not assumed to continue on its own.

It is also worth knowing what the organisation is actually worth, even without a sale on the table, since that number supports decisions on reinvestment, debt capacity and any buyout owed to a leader stepping back.
